editorNote: A police seizure turns a neighborhood bulletin board into a test of who is responsible for messages online, while Fido boards prepare to link up and novelists discover interactive fiction.
morningLine: Modems make a village—and bring the law to its door.

lead.headline: Police Seize a Bulletin Board: Is the Sysop Liable for What Users Post?
lead.dek: Los Angeles authorities confiscate MOG-UR’s HBBS equipment after telephone access codes appear among user messages.
body: Los Angeles police have seized the computer equipment behind MOG-UR’s HBBS, thrusting a three-year-old hobbyist bulletin board into an unfamiliar legal contest over responsibility for messages left by users. Pacific Telephone security investigators alerted police after finding a telephone credit-card code and two Sprint access numbers among posts on the system.

Officers took a Heathkit terminal, monitor, 5.25-inch floppy drive and roughly 150 disks from consultant and programmer Tom Tcimpidis. Felony charges remained under consideration by the district attorney. Tcimpidis said the board had been reached by about 5,000 users and held some 2,700 messages, and that he regularly warned callers not to post illicit material.

The central question reaches beyond one machine room: can a sysop reasonably be held liable for every item a caller places on an electronic board? Attorney Charles Lindner compared the case to blaming a supermarket for a notice pinned to its public bulletin board. The analogy fits a medium whose operators provide space but cannot continuously inspect a rapidly changing conversation.

Even the warrant hearing showed how new the territory is. Judge Robert Fratianne said WarGames helped him understand the problem. For the fast-growing BBS community, the seizure is both a warning about telephone fraud and an early test of whether the law can distinguish a system operator from the people using the system.

stories.headline: Fido Wants to Travel: Hobbyist Boards Begin to Form a Network
body: Hundreds of independent bulletin boards now serve local computer owners, but Tom Jennings wants his Fido software to carry mail between them. Eight Fido systems were operating from Missouri and Georgia to Oregon and Maui after Jennings put his own board online in November 1983 and shared the software.

Jennings expects networking software within about four months. Each board would call another during inexpensive late-night or weekend hours, compress addressed messages and pass them onward automatically—at a cost he estimated below a penny per message.

The plan points toward an electronic village larger than any single local telephone call. CompuServe already counted 130,000 members, while user groups such as the First Osborne Group were exploring links between boards and software libraries.

stories.headline: Novelists Move from Type to Bytes at Summer CES
body: At the June Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago, Spinnaker subsidiary Trillium introduced six adventures tied to major authors: Amazon, Rendezvous with Rama, Starman Jones, Fahrenheit 451, Dragonworld and Shadowkeep. Michael Crichton designed Amazon from a large flowchart, while Arthur C. Clarke, Robert Heinlein and Ray Bradbury supplied worlds already familiar to readers.

The projects treat interactive fiction as more than a licensed cover. Warner Books planned to release Alan Dean Foster’s Shadowkeep novel alongside the game, reversing the familiar path from book to adaptation. Apple II and Commodore 64 versions led the program, with several Atari editions planned.

Writers remain divided over what the machine can do. Crichton sees a new form waiting to be used more imaginatively; Bradbury cautions that a machine cannot reproduce the novel’s art of the aside. Their debate is becoming part of the game itself.

stories.headline: Morrow's Pivot Puts a PC-Compatible Computer on a Shoulder Strap
body: Morrow’s Pivot prototype abandons the bulky briefcase look for a narrow case carried by shoulder strap. Opening the flip-down keyboard reveals an 80-column, 16-line LCD, one or two one-third-height 5.25-inch drives and a built-in 300-baud modem.

Three MS-DOS configurations were promised for August at $2,500 to $3,000, weighing nine to 13 pounds. The base system carries 128K; a four-hour battery pack adds $50. IBM-style parallel, programmable serial and telephone connections are built in.

Lotus 1-2-3 ran without modification, though Flight Simulator did not because of the LCD’s graphics limitations. The compromise defines this road machine: business compatibility first, with shape and weight designed around how travelers actually carry computers.

stories.headline: Apple IIc Interest Runs Ahead of Complete Systems
body: Apple’s compact IIc is drawing attention faster than dealers can assemble complete systems. Product manager Ed Colby said allocations of green-screen monitors and second disk drives constrained sales, while Rainbow Computing reported that machines were not disappearing from shelves immediately.

Some IIe programs also stumbled over the IIc’s handling of spiral-recording and other copy-protection schemes, requiring continued testing and conversion. Apple expected a stronger back-to-school season; meanwhile, the reduced-price IIe was selling briskly at a $995 entry price.

worldAnchor.headline: Enrico Berlinguer Dies, Leaving Europe's Largest Communist Party Without Its Leader
worldAnchor.summary: Italian Communist Party chief Enrico Berlinguer died June 11 at age 62 after a cerebral hemorrhage suffered at a Padua rally. He had led the party since 1972 and was a principal figure in Eurocommunism.

bbsNote.headline: The Electronic Village Starts Linking Its Islands
bbsNote.summary: InfoWorld's June 18 communications package paired a legal warning—the seizure of a sysop's equipment—with evidence of extraordinary growth. Hundreds of BBSs, national service forums, user-group boards, and the first plans to connect independently run Fido systems were turning modems into a social medium.

posts.text: Tom Jennings said eight Fido systems were running around the country and described software under development to dial peer systems and exchange addressed mail automatically during low-rate hours.
CompuServe's 130,000-member service hosted forums for aviation, medicine, writing, and many other interests; forum sponsors supplied editorial labor while users paid for connect time.
The First Osborne Group used Bye, XModem, and Metal across two Daly City boards and was planning to network BBS access to its software library.
The same issue advertised a Hayes Smartmodem 1200 for $413-$489 and a Prometheus Pro-Modem 1200 for $359, showing the price of joining the online world.

curiosity.headline: Buy a DEC, Get an Apple Free
curiosity.summary: A San Jose dealer paired a business micro with a home machine in one of the period's stranger bundles.
curiosity.detail: ACP Technology Center advertised a DEC Rainbow 100 with 5MB hard disk at its $3,995 retail price and threw in an Apple IIe free; buyers of a $6,295 10MB Rainbow 100 Plus could receive a $1,295 Apple IIc. Sales manager Manny Lucro pitched the Apple as the educational family computer alongside DEC's business system.

gadgetWatch.headline: Compact Disc Players Crowd Summer Electronics Coverage
gadgetWatch.summary: Audio magazine's June 1984 equipment profile tested the Micro Seiki CD-M1, specifying 20Hz-20kHz response within plus/minus 0.5dB; Billboard's June 16 Summer CES report framed new audio and video technology as a central show theme.

undergroundDesk.headline: Phone-Fraud Posting Brings a BBS Seizure
undergroundDesk.dek: The MOG-UR case puts the underground’s posted access codes—and a sysop’s responsibility—before authorities.
body: Pacific Telephone investigators found a calling-card code and two Sprint access numbers among messages on MOG-UR’s HBBS. Los Angeles police responded by seizing the board’s hardware and disks while prosecutors weighed possible felony charges.

Tcimpidis said he did not know the data was present and routinely warned users against illicit posts. The episode shows the collision between open electronic conversation and enforcement against telephone fraud; no working codes or methods are reproduced here.
